subject: Computer Science
summary: Arrays, stacks, queues, linked lists, trees (binary trees, BST, AVL, heaps, B-trees), graphs, hashing, searching and sorting, with their complexities. This is one of the most heavily tested areas in DSSSB TGT Computer Science: expect traversal, BST/heap construction, hashing, sorting-pass and complexity questions.

sections.heading: Data structures and complexity basics
sections.body:
A **data structure** is a way of organising data in memory so that it can be used efficiently. An **Abstract Data Type (ADT)** specifies the data and operations (what), not the implementation (how); e.g. a Stack ADT can be implemented with an array or a linked list.
- **Linear**: array, stack, queue, linked list. **Non-linear**: tree, graph.
- **Static** (fixed size, array) vs **dynamic** (grows at run time, linked list).
The **efficiency** of an algorithm is measured by **time** and **space** complexity, expressed with asymptotic notation as a function of input size n: O (upper bound, usually the worst case), Ω (lower bound), Θ (tight bound).

sections.heading: Arrays and address calculation
sections.body:
An **array** stores elements of the **same type** in **contiguous** memory, so any element is reached in **O(1)** from its index (random access). Inserting or deleting in the middle needs shifting: O(n).
For a 1-D array A[LB..UB]: number of elements = UB - LB + 1, and LOC(A[i]) = B + w(i - LB), where B is the base address and w the size of one element in bytes.
A 2-D array A[M][N] is stored either:
- **Row-major** (row by row): used by **C, C++, Java, Python (NumPy default)**.
- **Column-major** (column by column): used by **FORTRAN**, MATLAB.
In C (lower bounds 0), row-major gives LOC(A[i][j]) = B + w(i × N + j).
A **sparse matrix** (mostly zeros) is stored as (row, column, value) triplets. A triangular n × n matrix has n(n + 1)/2 non-zero positions.

sections.heading: Stacks
sections.body:
A **stack** is a linear structure where insertion (**push**) and deletion (**pop**) happen at **one end only**, the **top**. It is **LIFO** (Last In, First Out). `peek`/`top` reads the top element without removing it. All three operations are **O(1)**.
Array implementation: `top = -1` means empty; **overflow** is a push when top = MAX - 1, **underflow** a pop from an empty stack.
Applications: function calls and **recursion** (call stack of activation records), infix-to-postfix conversion and **postfix evaluation**, balanced-parentheses checking, undo, backtracking and **DFS**, reversing a string.
With pops allowed between pushes of 1, 2, 3 (in that order), 5 output orders are possible (Catalan number); 3, 1, 2 is impossible.

sections.heading: Infix, prefix and postfix expressions
sections.body:
**Infix** `A + B`, **prefix (Polish)** `+ A B`, **postfix (Reverse Polish)** `A B +`. Prefix and postfix need no brackets.
**Infix → postfix with a stack** (scan left to right):
- Operand → write it to the output.
- `(` → push. `)` → pop to output until `(` is found; discard both brackets.
- Operator → pop to output every operator on top with **higher precedence**, or **equal precedence if the incoming operator is left-associative**; then push the incoming operator. (`^` is right-associative, so an incoming `^` does not pop another `^`.)
- At the end, pop all remaining operators.
Precedence: `^` > `* / %` > `+ -`.
**Postfix evaluation**: push operands; on an operator, pop **two** values (the first popped is the **right** operand), apply, push the result. The final value on the stack is the answer.
Example: A + B * (C - D) / E → postfix **A B C D - * E / +**, prefix **+ A / * B - C D E**.

sections.heading: Queues, circular queues, deques and priority queues
sections.body:
A **queue** is **FIFO** (First In, First Out): insertion (**enqueue**) at the **rear**, deletion (**dequeue**) at the **front**, both O(1).
In a simple array queue, freed front slots are never reused. A **circular queue** wraps indices: `rear = (rear + 1) % N`. With one slot kept empty, it is **full when (rear + 1) % N == front** and **empty when front == rear** (some books use front = -1 for empty; follow the question's convention).
Variants:
- **Deque** (double-ended queue): insert and delete at both ends. **Input-restricted** deque: insertion at one end only; **output-restricted**: deletion at one end only.
- **Priority queue**: the element with the highest priority is removed first; efficiently implemented with a **binary heap** (insert and delete in O(log n)).
Applications: CPU scheduling, printer spooling, buffers, **BFS**, level-order traversal.

sections.heading: Linked lists
sections.body:
A **linked list** is a linear collection of **nodes**; each node holds data and a pointer (link) to the next node. A `head` pointer locates the first node; the last node's link is NULL.
- **Singly linked**: one `next` pointer; traversal in one direction only.
- **Doubly linked**: `prev` and `next` pointers; two-way traversal, and a node can be deleted in O(1) when a pointer to it is given.
- **Circular**: the last node points back to the first (no NULL); useful for round-robin scheduling.
- **Header linked list**: a special header node at the start.
Versus arrays: dynamic size and O(1) insertion/deletion at a known position, but **no random access**, extra memory for pointers and no efficient binary search.
Insert at head O(1); at tail O(n) unless a tail pointer is kept; search O(n); reversal O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.heading: Trees and binary tree properties
sections.body:
A **tree** is a hierarchical structure with one **root**; every other node has exactly one **parent**. Terms: **leaf**, **internal node**, **siblings**, **degree** (number of children), **level** (root at 0), **height** (longest root-to-leaf path). n nodes → **n - 1 edges**.
Here height counts **edges** (single node = 0); some books count levels (single node = 1).
A **binary tree** allows at most two children (left, right). Types:
- **Full/strict**: every node has 0 or 2 children.
- **Complete**: all levels full except possibly the last, which is filled **from the left**.
- **Perfect**: all internal nodes have 2 children and all leaves are at the same level.
- **Skewed**: every node has only one child (behaves like a linked list).
Properties (see formulas): max nodes 2ʰ⁺¹ - 1, min h + 1, n₀ = n₂ + 1, n + 1 NULL links, minimum height ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ - 1. Complete trees (heaps) are stored in arrays: children of i at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

sections.heading: Tree traversals
sections.body:
Depth-first traversals (recursive, or with an explicit stack):
- **Preorder**: Node, Left, Right (NLR).
- **Inorder**: Left, Node, Right (LNR). For a **BST it gives keys in ascending order**.
- **Postorder**: Left, Right, Node (LRN). Used to delete a tree or evaluate an expression tree.
**Level-order** (breadth-first) visits level by level using a **queue**.
In an **expression tree**, preorder/inorder/postorder give prefix/infix/postfix.
**Reconstruction**: inorder together with preorder or postorder identifies a binary tree uniquely. Preorder + postorder alone is not enough in general (it is enough for a full binary tree). For a **BST**, preorder or postorder alone is enough, because the inorder is just the sorted keys.
For "new-order" questions apply the given order recursively; Right-Node-Left on a BST gives descending order.

code.source:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data, left=None, right=None):
        self.data, self.left, self.right = data, left, right

def preorder(n):  return [n.data] + preorder(n.left) + preorder(n.right) if n else []
def inorder(n):   return inorder(n.left) + [n.data] + inorder(n.right) if n else []
def postorder(n): return postorder(n.left) + postorder(n.right) + [n.data] if n else []
def levelorder(root):
    out, queue = [], [root]
    while queue:
        n = queue.pop(0)
        out.append(n.data)
        queue += [c for c in (n.left, n.right) if c]
    return out

root = Node('A', Node('B', Node('D'), Node('E', Node('G'))),
                 Node('C', None, Node('F')))
for f in (preorder, inorder, postorder, levelorder):
    print(f.__name__, ' '.join(f(root)))

sections.heading: Binary search trees
sections.body:
A **binary search tree (BST)** is a binary tree in which, for every node N, all keys in the **left subtree are less than N** and all keys in the **right subtree are greater than N** (if duplicates are allowed, the book's convention decides which side they go). Both subtrees are BSTs.
- **Insert**: search for the key, attach it as a leaf where the search ends.
- **Minimum** = leftmost node; **maximum** = rightmost; **inorder is sorted**.
**Deletion** of node N:
- **No child (leaf)**: replace the parent's pointer to N by NULL.
- **One child**: link N's parent directly to N's only child.
- **Two children**: replace N's key with its **inorder successor** (smallest key in the right subtree) or **inorder predecessor** (largest key in the left subtree), then delete that node, which has at most one child.
All operations take **O(h)**: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) for a **skewed** tree (e.g. keys inserted in sorted order).

sections.heading: AVL trees, red-black trees, B-trees and heaps
sections.body:
**AVL tree** (Adelson-Velsky and Landis): a self-balancing BST in which every node's **balance factor** BF = height(left subtree) - height(right subtree) is **-1, 0 or +1**. After an insertion or deletion that makes |BF| = 2, rotations restore balance:
- **LL** case → single **right** rotation; **RR** case → single **left** rotation (single rotations).
- **LR** case → left then right rotation; **RL** case → right then left rotation (**double rotations**).
Search, insert and delete are **O(log n)**.
**Red-black tree**: root black, no red node has a red child, equal black nodes on every root-to-NULL path; height **≤ 2 log₂(n + 1)**.
**B-tree of order m** (database indexes): at most m children and m - 1 keys per node; internal non-root nodes have at least ⌈m/2⌉ children; all leaves at the same level. A **B+ tree** keeps records only in linked leaves.
**Binary heap**: a **complete binary tree** stored in an array. **Max-heap**: every parent ≥ its children (root = maximum); **min-heap**: parent ≤ children. Insert: add at the end, then **sift up**, O(log n). Delete root: move the last element to the root, then **sift down**, O(log n). Building a heap bottom-up from n elements takes **O(n)**; heap sort takes O(n log n).

sections.heading: Graphs: terminology and representation
sections.body:
A **graph** G = (V, E): vertices and edges; **directed** or **undirected**, weighted or not. A **simple graph** has no self-loops or parallel edges.
- **Degree** of a vertex = number of edges incident on it (a self-loop counts 2). In a digraph, in-degree and out-degree. Degree 0 = **isolated** vertex; degree 1 = **pendant** vertex.
- **Handshaking lemma**: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|, so the sum of degrees is even and the **number of odd-degree vertices is even**. In a digraph, Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E|.
- A **complete graph** Kₙ has n(n - 1)/2 edges (max for a simple undirected graph); a simple digraph can have n(n - 1).
- A **tree** is a connected acyclic graph (n - 1 edges); a **DAG** is a directed acyclic graph. A **spanning tree** has all n vertices and n - 1 edges; Kₙ has nⁿ⁻² of them (Cayley).
Representations:
- **Adjacency matrix**: V × V, entry 1 (or weight) if an edge exists; symmetric for undirected graphs; O(V²) space; O(1) edge test.
- **Adjacency list**: a list of neighbours per vertex; O(V + E) space; best for sparse graphs.
- **Incidence matrix**: V × E.
**BFS** (queue) and **DFS** (stack) take O(V + E) with lists, O(V²) with a matrix.

sections.heading: Hashing
sections.body:
**Hashing** stores a key at an index computed by a **hash function** h(k) in a **hash table** of size m, giving **O(1) average** search, insert and delete.
Hash functions:
- **Division**: h(k) = k mod m (m preferably a prime not close to a power of 2).
- **Mid-square** (middle digits of k²), **folding** (split the key into parts and add them), **multiplication** h(k) = ⌊m × (kA mod 1)⌋.
A **collision** occurs when two keys hash to the same index. Resolution techniques:
- **Separate chaining (open hashing)**: each slot holds a linked list; load factor may exceed 1.
- **Open addressing (closed hashing)**: probe other slots in the table itself. **Linear probing**: (h(k) + i) mod m, which causes **primary clustering**. **Quadratic probing**: (h(k) + i²) mod m, which causes **secondary clustering**. **Double hashing**: (h₁(k) + i × h₂(k)) mod m, with h₂(k) ≠ 0.
**Load factor** α = n/m; open addressing needs α ≤ 1. **Rehashing** builds a bigger table and re-inserts all keys when α crosses a threshold.

sections.heading: Searching: linear and binary search
sections.body:
**Linear (sequential) search** checks elements one by one. It works on unsorted data and on linked lists. Best case 1 comparison, worst n, average about (n + 1)/2 for a successful search: **O(n)**.
**Binary search** requires a **sorted** list with **direct (random) access** to the middle element (an array, not a linked list). Compare the key with A[mid]: equal → found; key smaller → search the left half (high = mid - 1); key larger → search the right half (low = mid + 1). The search is **unsuccessful when low > high** (Beg > End).
- mid = (low + high)/2, or low + (high - low)/2 to avoid integer overflow.
- At most **⌊log₂n⌋ + 1** comparisons: **O(log n)** worst and average, O(1) best. For n = 1000 the maximum is 10.
**Interpolation search**: O(log log n) average for uniformly distributed keys, O(n) worst.

sections.heading: Sorting algorithms
sections.body:
- **Bubble sort**: repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; after pass k the k largest elements are in their final places. With a "swapped" flag it stops early (best case O(n) on sorted input). The number of swaps equals the number of **inversions**.
- **Selection sort**: in pass i, select the minimum of the unsorted part and swap it into position i. Always O(n²) comparisons but at most n - 1 swaps.
- **Insertion sort**: insert each element into the sorted part on its left. Best O(n) on nearly sorted data; good for small inputs.
- **Merge sort**: divide into halves, sort, merge; always O(n log n); needs O(n) extra space; stable.
- **Quick sort**: partition around a pivot; O(n log n) on average but **O(n²) worst case** (e.g. sorted input with the first or last element as pivot).
- **Heap sort**: build a max-heap, repeatedly move the root to the end; O(n log n), in place, not stable.
- **Counting / radix sort** are not comparison based; radix (LSD) sorts digit by digit from the least significant, using a stable sort.
A **stable** sort keeps equal keys in their original order. Comparison sorts need **Ω(n log n)** comparisons in the worst case.

workedExamples.problem: A[1..10][1..15] is an integer array with 4 bytes per element and base address 2000. Find the address of A[4][7] in (a) row-major and (b) column-major order.
Convert the infix expression A * (B + C) - D / E to postfix using a stack, and give its prefix form.
workedExamples.solution:
Scan left to right (output | stack):
- A → output A | stack empty
- * → push | *
- ( → push | * (
- B → A B | * (
- + → push (top is '(') | * ( +
- C → A B C | * ( +
- ) → pop + → A B C + | *
- - → * has higher precedence, pop it → A B C + * ; push - | -
- D → A B C + * D | -
- / → / is higher than -, so push | - /
- E → A B C + * D E | - /
- End: pop / then - → **A B C + * D E / -**
Prefix (convert inner parts first): B + C → + B C; A * (..) → * A + B C; D / E → / D E; whole → **- * A + B C / D E**

workedExamples.problem: The inorder traversal of a binary tree is D B E A F C G and its preorder traversal is A B D E C F G. Draw the tree and find its postorder traversal.
workedExamples.solution:
- Preorder starts with the root: **A**. In the inorder, D B E lies left of A and F C G lies right.
- Left part: the next preorder element among {D, B, E} is **B**, so B is the root of the left subtree; in the inorder, D is left of B and E is right.
- Right part: the next preorder element among {F, C, G} is **C**; F is its left child and G its right child.
Tree: A has children B and C; B has children D and E; C has children F and G.
Postorder (Left, Right, Node): **D E B F G C A**

workedExamples.problem: Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 35 into an empty BST. Give the preorder traversal. Then delete 30 (using the inorder successor) and give the new preorder and inorder traversals.
workedExamples.solution:
Building the tree: 50 is the root; 30 and 70 are its children; 20 and 40 are children of 30; 60 and 80 are children of 70; 35 < 50 → left, > 30 → right, < 40 → left child of 40.
Preorder: **50 30 20 40 35 70 60 80**
Delete 30 (two children): its inorder successor is the minimum of its right subtree {40, 35} = **35**. Copy 35 into 30's place and delete the old leaf 35.
New tree: 50 → (35 → 20, 40), (70 → 60, 80).
Preorder: **50 35 20 40 70 60 80**; inorder: **20 35 40 50 60 70 80** (still sorted).

workedExamples.problem: Insert the keys 12, 22, 35, 42, 19, 29, 9 into a hash table of size 10 using h(k) = k mod 10 and linear probing. Show the final table and the number of probes needed for 9.
workedExamples.solution:
- 12 → 2 (free) → slot 2
- 22 → 2 taken → 3 → slot 3
- 35 → 5 → slot 5
- 42 → 2, 3 taken → 4 → slot 4
- 19 → 9 → slot 9
- 29 → 9 taken → (9 + 1) mod 10 = 0 → slot 0
- 9 → 9 taken, 0 taken → 1 → slot 1
Final table: 0:29, 1:9, 2:12, 3:22, 4:42, 5:35, 6:-, 7:-, 8:-, 9:19.
Key 9 was placed after examining slots 9, 0, 1: **3 probes**. Note the cluster at slots 9, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: primary clustering.

workedExamples.problem: The max-heap [90, 70, 80, 30, 60, 50, 40] is stored in an array. Insert 85 and give the new array. Then delete the root from the new heap and give the result.
workedExamples.solution:
Use 1-based positions: parent of i is ⌊i/2⌋.
Insert 85 at position 8: its parent is position 4 (30). 85 > 30 → swap (85 now at 4). Parent is position 2 (70): 85 > 70 → swap (85 at 2). Parent is position 1 (90): 85 < 90 → stop.
After insertion: **[90, 85, 80, 70, 60, 50, 40, 30]**
Delete root 90: move the last element 30 to the root → [30, 85, 80, 70, 60, 50, 40]. Sift down: the larger child of 30 is 85 → swap → [85, 30, 80, 70, 60, 50, 40]; children of 30 (position 2) are 70 and 60, larger is 70 → swap → [85, 70, 80, 30, 60, 50, 40]; 30 is now a leaf.
After deletion: **[85, 70, 80, 30, 60, 50, 40]**

pitfalls: Height conventions differ: with height in edges a single node has height 0 and max nodes = 2ʰ⁺¹ - 1; with height in levels it is 2ʰ - 1. Read the question's definition.
Binary search needs sorted data and random access; it is not efficient on a linked list.
In postfix evaluation the first value popped is the right operand: for '8 2 /' compute 8 / 2, not 2 / 8.
^ is right-associative: A ^ B ^ C becomes A B C ^ ^ in postfix, not A B ^ C ^.
Quick sort's worst case is O(n²), which occurs on already sorted input when the first or last element is the pivot.
Selection sort, quick sort and heap sort are not stable; bubble, insertion, merge, counting and radix sort are.
Preorder plus postorder does not uniquely define a general binary tree; inorder is needed (except for full binary trees or BSTs).
Folding and mid-square are hash functions, not collision-resolution techniques; rehashing resizes the table.
An AVL balance factor of ±2 means the tree is unbalanced; only -1, 0, +1 are valid.
Building a heap from n elements is O(n), not O(n log n); inserting n elements one at a time is O(n log n).
Row-major is used by C/C++/Java and column-major by FORTRAN; swapping them gives a wrong address.
quickRevision: Stack = LIFO (push/pop at top); queue = FIFO (enqueue at rear, dequeue at front).
Recursion, expression conversion, parenthesis matching and DFS use stacks; BFS and scheduling use queues.
Circular queue full: (rear + 1) mod N == front (one-slot-empty convention).
Linked list: O(1) insertion at head, O(n) search, no random access.
Binary tree: n₀ = n₂ + 1; n nodes have n - 1 edges and n + 1 NULL links.
Preorder NLR, inorder LNR, postorder LRN; inorder of a BST is sorted.
BST operations are O(h): O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when skewed.
Deleting a BST node with two children: replace it by its inorder successor or predecessor.
AVL: BF ∈ {-1, 0, +1}; LL and RR need single rotations, LR and RL need double rotations.
Heap: complete binary tree; insert and delete O(log n); build-heap O(n).
Sum of degrees = 2E; the number of odd-degree vertices is always even; degree-1 vertex = pendant.
Adjacency matrix O(V²) space; adjacency list O(V + E).
Linear probing → primary clustering; quadratic probing → secondary clustering.
Merge sort is stable and always O(n log n); quick sort worst case O(n²).
